body.heading: It really does look bigger — but it isn't
paragraphs: Watch the Moon rise on a clear evening and it can look enormous, looming over rooftops and treetops. A few hours later, high in the sky, the same Moon looks small and ordinary. Nothing about the Moon has changed: it is about 384,400 kilometres away either way, and it covers the same tiny patch of sky — roughly the width of your thumbnail at arm's length.

So why does it look so different? The Moon illusion, as scientists call it, is a trick of your brain, not of the sky. When the Moon sits near the horizon, your brain compares it with houses, trees and hills, and judges it to be huge. High overhead there is nothing to compare it with, so it shrinks in your mind's eye.

body.heading: A simple test you can try
paragraphs: Next time the rising Moon looks giant, hold your thumb up at arm's length and compare the Moon to your thumbnail. Then do the same when the Moon is high overhead later that night. Your thumbnail is the same size both times — and so is the Moon. Photographs prove it too: a camera has no brain to fool, and the Moon measures the same in both pictures.

Scientists still argue about exactly which part of the brain is responsible, but the effect itself is one of the oldest known optical illusions. It is a good reminder that seeing is not just what your eyes do — it is what your brain decides your eyes mean.
